transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

I work as a healthcare operations manager, and I've been really struggling with my focus lately. During long meetings or when I’m working through complex plans, my mind keeps drifting off and I miss important details even though I’m really trying to pay attention. It's starting to impact my work, so I wanted to get some professional advice.
In addition to the focus problems, have you been feeling down, depressed, or losing interest or pleasure in things most days lately?

No, I wouldn't say I'm depressed or losing interest at all. I actually care deeply about my work and my community projects, but I just feel really frustrated and overwhelmed by how hard it is to stay focused lately.
Did you have similar attention or distractibility problems as a child or teenager, before age 12, or is this a new problem that started only recently?

These issues actually go all the way back to my childhood. Even in elementary school, my teachers would write on my report cards that I was bright but always daydreaming, losing worksheets, and forgetting to turn in homework. My parents used to joke that I’d forget my head if it wasn't attached.
Do these attention and forgetfulness problems happen in more than one setting, such as both at work and at home or in social situations?

Yes, absolutely, it's definitely not just limited to my day job. At home, I'm constantly forgetting to pay bills on time and my phone is cluttered with half-written reminders just so I don't lose track of basic personal errands. It also spills into my volunteer roles, where I've completely missed community board meetings or gotten totally sidetracked while trying to plan our local health fairs.
Do you also have symptoms of hyperactivity or impulsivity, such as feeling restless, fidgeting, interrupting others, or acting before thinking?

I don't really feel physically restless or fidgety, but I definitely struggle with talking too much and interrupting others. In smaller meetings or community groups, I tend to dominate conversations, talk over people, and give way more detail than anyone asked for. I usually only realize I'm doing it when I notice others checking the clock or not jumping in.
Do these talking too much and interrupting behaviors cause problems in your daily life, such as at work, in relationships, or in meetings?

Yes, it definitely causes some social awkwardness, particularly in my smaller committee and community meetings. I often catch myself talking over people and giving way too much detail, only realizing I've been dominating the conversation when I notice others looking at the clock. It leaves me feeling quite embarrassed and worried that I'm frustrating the very people I want to work closely with.
Before age 12, did these attention problems and interrupting/talking-too-much behaviors cause noticeable difficulties at school, at home, or with friends?

Yes, they definitely caused some issues even back then. In elementary school, my teachers frequently noted on my report cards that I was bright but always daydreaming, losing my worksheets, and forgetting to turn in completed homework. At home, my constant forgetfulness led my parents to joke that I'd forget my head if it wasn't attached to my shoulders.
Do you also often feel physically restless or unable to sit still, such as fidgeting, tapping, leaving your seat, or feeling driven to move around?

No, I don't really experience physical restlessness, fidgeting, or a need to constantly move around. I've never really been someone who taps their feet or feels the urge to get up and pace. My struggles are much more about my mind wandering rather than my body needing to move.
Do these focus and impulsive talking problems make it hard for you to complete tasks on time or lead to mistakes at work, home, or in daily responsibilities?

Yes, they definitely cause mistakes; I often send out spreadsheets with incorrect date ranges or wrong column sums because I skimmed them, and I'll constantly bounce between different tasks without actually finishing them in a logical order. It's gotten to the point where coworkers quietly double-check my work and take over pieces of projects, which has even led me to turn down new leadership roles because I'm worried I can't reliably keep everything straight anymore.
Do you also often make impulsive decisions or act without thinking, such as blurting things out, interrupting others, spending impulsively, or doing things that later cause problems?

I don't really struggle with impulsive spending or reckless actions, but I definitely have issues with conversational impulsivity. During meetings or community projects, I often catch myself talking over people, dominating the conversation, and sharing way too much detail. I usually only realize I've done it when I notice others looking at the clock.
Do you also often feel very restless inside, like you have to move or cannot sit still, even if you are not physically fidgeting?

No, I don't really experience that kind of internal restlessness or a constant need to move. My struggles are almost entirely with my mind drifting off rather than any kind of physical or internal restlessness.
Have you ever had a period of several days or more when your energy felt unusually high, you needed much less sleep, and you were more talkative or impulsive than usual?

No, I've never had periods of unusually high energy or a decreased need for sleep like that. My talkativeness is really more about getting overly excited about work projects I care about, rather than feeling manic or impulsive.
Do you often make careless mistakes, lose things, or forget everyday tasks because you’re distracted or not fully following through?

Yes, I often make careless mistakes at work, like sending out spreadsheets with incorrect dates or formula errors because I skimmed them instead of reading carefully. I also constantly forget everyday tasks like returning phone calls or paying bills, which is a habit that goes back to my childhood when I was always losing school worksheets and forgetting homework.
Do these attention and impulsivity symptoms happen in a way that clearly interferes with your life in more than one area, such as work, home, and social situations?

Yes, they absolutely affect multiple areas of my life. At work, colleagues have started quietly double-checking my work, and I've even turned down new leadership roles because of my self-doubt. Meanwhile, in my personal and community life, I constantly forget to pay bills, miss board meetings despite reminders, and tend to talk over people or dominate conversations in social groups.
Do you think these attention problems and interrupting/talking too much have been present continuously since childhood, or do they come and go in episodes?

They have definitely been a continuous, long-standing pattern since childhood rather than coming in episodes. Even back in elementary school, I was always daydreaming and losing worksheets, but the struggles have become much more noticeable over the last two years as my responsibilities expanded.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets criteria for ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation, with some hyperactive/impulsive features (talking too much, interrupting) but no prominent physical hyperactivity. Symptoms began in childhood, are present in multiple settings, are continuous rather than episodic, and cause clear occupational and social impairment.
